items.prompt: What role does slightly acidic rainwater play in starting a limestone cave?

options.label: It seeps into existing cracks in the rock and slowly dissolves the limestone along the way, widening those cracks into passages over an immense span of time
options.feedback: Repeated over an enormous stretch of time, that slow dissolving is exactly what opens a crack into a passage.

options.label: It washes away loose sand that was already filling open passages
options.feedback: A young limestone cave does not begin as a passage already open and filled with sand; the passage itself has to be carved out of solid rock first.

options.label: It freezes inside cracks and splits the rock apart instantly
options.feedback: That describes a much faster mechanical process unrelated to dissolving; a limestone cave forms through slow chemical dissolving, not sudden freezing and cracking.

options.label: It simply flows over the surface of the rock without ever entering it
options.feedback: Water that only stays on the surface cannot dissolve rock hidden below it; the water has to seep into cracks and reach the rock directly to dissolve it.

items.ok_line: Widened, crack by crack, over an immense span of time.
items.ko_title: Not sand, not freezing, not surface flow alone
items.ko_line: Ask where the water actually has to go to reach the rock it dissolves.
items.exp_text: Rainwater that has become slightly acidic seeps down into the natural cracks already running through a bed of limestone, and as it does, it slowly dissolves a little of the rock it touches along the way. Repeated again and again over an enormous span of time, that slow dissolving widens the same cracks bit by bit until they have opened into passages large enough to walk through.

items.prompt: Why is rainwater capable of dissolving solid limestone at all, when pure water alone barely touches it?

options.label: Rainwater is naturally warmer than groundwater, and warmth alone dissolves limestone
options.feedback: Rainwater is not reliably warmer than groundwater, and temperature alone is not what gives it the ability to dissolve limestone; its acidity is.

options.label: As it falls and seeps into the ground, rain picks up carbon dioxide from the air and the soil, turning it into a weak acid
options.feedback: That absorbed carbon dioxide is exactly what turns ordinary rain into something able to slowly dissolve limestone.

options.label: Rainwater carries fine sand that grinds the limestone away mechanically
options.feedback: Grinding away rock with sand would be a mechanical process, not dissolving; the process at work here is chemical, driven by acidity, not grit.

options.label: Limestone itself slowly turns into water on contact with any moisture
options.feedback: Limestone does not transform directly into water; it is dissolved by a mildly acidic solution and carried away as dissolved material, not converted into water itself.

items.ok_line: A weak acid, picked up along the way down.
items.ko_title: Not warmth, not grit, not a direct transformation
items.ko_line: Ask what the water absorbs on its way from the air, through the soil, and into the rock.
items.exp_title: A weak acid, picked up along the way
items.exp_text: As raindrops fall through the air and then seep down through soil, they absorb carbon dioxide from both, and that carbon dioxide reacts with the water to form a weak acid. Even though the acid is far too mild to do anything dramatic in a hurry, it is exactly strong enough to slowly dissolve limestone, given the amount of time the water spends seeping through it.

items.prompt: How does a stalactite grow downward from a cave ceiling?

options.label: It grows the same way an icicle does, by water simply freezing solid
options.feedback: A stalactite is not frozen water; it is built from mineral left behind, and it keeps growing even where a cave never gets cold enough to freeze.

options.label: A single drop of water hangs permanently from the ceiling and slowly hardens in place
options.feedback: A stalactite is not one drop that hardens; it is built from countless separate drops, one after another, each leaving a little material behind before falling.

options.label: Mineral-laden water dripping from the ceiling leaves a tiny trace of dissolved mineral behind each time, building up drop by drop from the ceiling downward
options.feedback: Each drop deposits its own tiny trace of mineral before falling, and that trace slowly builds downward over time.

options.label: Dust from the cave air slowly settles and sticks to the ceiling over time
options.feedback: Settling dust would not reliably build a pointed shape hanging from one exact spot on the ceiling; the shape comes from mineral left behind by water at that same point, again and again.

items.ko_title: Not ice, not one drop, not dust
items.ko_line: Think about what a single drop leaves behind right before it falls away.
items.exp_text: Water seeping through the rock above a cave ceiling carries dissolved mineral with it, and where it reaches open air at the tip of a crack, a tiny trace of that mineral is left behind before the drop finally falls. Because the next drop forms at exactly the same spot and leaves its own tiny trace in turn, that mineral slowly builds downward from the ceiling, one drop's worth at a time.

items.prompt: How does a stalagmite form on a cave floor, growing upward rather than down?

options.label: It grows from mineral rising up out of the floor itself, unrelated to any water dripping onto it
options.feedback: The mineral does not rise up from within the floor; it is carried in by drops of water landing on the floor from above.

options.label: It forms only where a stalactite above it has already fully finished growing
options.feedback: A stalagmite can keep growing on the floor while the stalactite above it is still actively forming too; neither one needs to already be finished.

options.label: It is built from dust that drifts down and piles up in one spot
options.feedback: Piling dust would not reliably keep growing at one exact point beneath a drip; the growth is driven by mineral carried in dripping water, not settling dust.

options.label: Each drop landing on the floor beneath a drip point leaves behind a tiny trace of mineral before soaking in or evaporating, and that trace builds upward over time
options.feedback: Drop after drop landing at the same spot slowly builds a mound reaching up from the floor.

items.ok_line: Built upward, drop by drop, at the same spot the water lands.
items.ko_title: Not rising rock, not a finished stalactite, not dust
items.ko_line: Ask what a drop leaves behind right where it lands on the floor.
items.exp_text: A drop that falls from the ceiling and lands on the same spot on the floor below carries the same dissolved mineral that the stalactite above is being built from. As each drop lands, splashes slightly, and then either soaks in or evaporates, it leaves behind a tiny trace of that mineral right where it landed, and repeated drop after drop, that trace slowly builds up into a mound reaching upward from the floor.

items.prompt: What happens when a stalactite and a stalagmite eventually meet after growing toward each other for long enough?

options.label: They join into a single column linking the floor to the ceiling
options.feedback: Once they touch, the mineral each was made of connects into one unbroken structure running from floor to ceiling.

options.label: One of the two immediately dissolves away completely
options.feedback: Meeting does not cause either formation to dissolve away; both simply continue being built up by the same dripping water, now joined into one.

options.label: They separate again as soon as they touch, pushed apart by the weight of new drops
options.feedback: Once joined, the two formations stay connected; new drops continue adding mineral to the now-single connected structure rather than pushing it apart.

options.label: The dripping water stops permanently the moment they touch
options.feedback: The water that built both formations does not stop simply because they have met; it can keep depositing mineral onto the joined structure.

items.ok_line: Two formations, joined into one column.
items.ko_title: Not dissolved, not pushed apart, not stopped
items.ko_line: Both formations are made of the same material, deposited by the same dripping water; ask what happens once they touch.
items.exp_text: A stalactite reaching down from the ceiling and a stalagmite reaching up from the floor below it are both built by the very same dripping water, so as long as that dripping continues, both keep growing toward each other. Once they finally touch, the mineral each was made of connects into a single unbroken column running from floor to ceiling, and dripping water continuing to reach that spot only keeps adding to it.

items.prompt: How does flowstone form, and why does its shape follow the exact path water takes across a surface?

options.label: It forms from water dripping from a single fixed point, the same way a stalactite does
options.feedback: Flowstone is built by water flowing and spreading across a surface, not by drops falling repeatedly from one fixed point overhead.

options.label: Mineral is deposited by water flowing over a surface rather than dripping from one point, so the deposit traces the exact path the water spreads across, layer after layer
options.feedback: Wherever the flowing water actually touches the surface, it leaves mineral behind, tracing its own path.

options.label: It forms only where a cave floor has already frozen solid
options.feedback: Flowstone forms regardless of freezing; it is built from mineral carried by liquid water flowing across a surface, not from ice.

options.label: It is carved out of solid rock by the mechanical scraping of moving water
options.feedback: Flowstone is not solid rock that gets carved away; it is new mineral material being added onto a surface as water flows across it.

items.ok_line: Left wherever the water actually spread.
items.ko_title: Not one drip point, not ice, not carving
items.ko_line: Ask whether the water here is falling from one spot, or spreading across a surface.
items.exp_text: Instead of falling as separate drops from one fixed spot, the water that builds flowstone spreads out and runs across a broader surface, carrying dissolved mineral along with it. As that water thins and slows across the rock, it leaves mineral behind all along the surface it actually touches, so the deposit that builds up follows precisely the path the flowing water took.

items.prompt: Why do caves tend to stay at a steady temperature year-round, largely unaffected by outside weather?

options.label: Underground rivers constantly pump in air of a fixed temperature
options.feedback: It is not an active pumping of fixed-temperature air that keeps a cave steady; the surrounding rock itself is what holds the temperature in place.

options.label: Caves generate their own heat that overpowers any outside weather
options.feedback: Caves do not produce their own heat in any meaningful amount; their steadiness comes from being shielded from outside swings, not from generating warmth.

options.label: The rock and earth above a cave insulate it, cutting it off from the swings in temperature that happen at the surface
options.feedback: That thick layer of insulating rock and soil smooths out the surface's daily and seasonal swings before they can reach the cave.

options.label: Cave air is replaced completely with fresh air every day, resetting its temperature
options.feedback: Deep cave air is not fully replaced on a daily basis; its steadiness comes from insulation, not from constant fresh air exchange.

items.ok_line: Shielded from the weather above by rock and earth.
items.ko_title: Not pumped air, not self-heating, not daily replacement
items.ko_line: Ask what actually stands between a cave and the changing weather at the surface.
items.exp_text: The surface above a cave heats up in the day and in summer, and cools at night and in winter, but rock and soil are slow to let that changing heat pass through them. By the time any of that surface swing could reach a cave sitting well beneath a thick layer of insulating rock, it has been smoothed out almost entirely, leaving the air inside close to one steady temperature.

items.prompt: Why have many cave-dwelling animals that live in permanent darkness lost their eyes over many generations?

options.label: Darkness directly damages the eyes of every generation born in a cave
options.feedback: Darkness by itself does not physically injure an animal's eyes; the loss shows up gradually across generations, not as damage within a single lifetime.

options.label: Eyes are removed on purpose by other cave animals competing for food
options.feedback: Nothing in a cave is deliberately removing another animal's eyes; the change happens without any such direct action.

options.label: Cave animals evolve faster than animals living anywhere else
options.feedback: There is no reason cave populations would change from generation to generation any faster in general; what differs is which traits stop mattering in the dark, not the overall pace of change.

options.label: In permanent darkness, working eyes give no advantage over the generations, so a population is not held back by losing them
options.feedback: With nothing for a working eye to see, an animal born with weaker eyes is at no real disadvantage compared to one born with better ones.

items.ok_line: No advantage left in the dark, so none is preserved.
items.ko_title: Not damage, not removal, not faster change overall
items.ko_line: Ask whether a working eye actually helps an animal in a place with no light at all.
items.exp_text: In a place with no light at all, an eye capable of seeing has nothing to see, so an animal born with slightly weaker eyes is at no real disadvantage compared to one born with better ones. Across many generations in a population where that difference no longer matters, working eyes can be lost without it costing the population anything, even though the same loss would be a serious problem anywhere light still reaches.

items.prompt: How do bats find their way and hunt in the pitch-black parts of a cave?

options.label: They emit sounds and listen for the echoes bouncing back off obstacles and prey, building a sense of their surroundings without needing any light
options.feedback: Comparing the timing and direction of each returning echo lets a bat build a working sense of what surrounds it, moment to moment.

options.label: They can see using a kind of vision that works even in complete darkness
options.feedback: No eye can form an image where there is no light at all to work with; bats flying in total darkness rely on something other than sight.

options.label: They follow scent trails left behind by other bats on previous flights
options.feedback: Navigating cave passages and catching moving prey in complete darkness by scent alone would be far too slow and imprecise for what a bat actually does.

options.label: They memorize the exact layout of the cave and never actually sense anything as they fly
options.feedback: Memory alone could not account for a bat catching prey that is itself moving unpredictably; something in the moment has to be sensing where things currently are.

items.ok_line: Finding the way by sound alone.
items.ko_title: Not dark-vision, not scent, not memory alone
items.ko_line: Ask what a bat sends out into the darkness, and what comes back to it.
items.exp_title: Finding the way by sound alone
items.exp_text: A bat flying through total darkness sends out a rapid stream of sounds and listens for the echoes that bounce back from whatever those sounds strike, whether that is a cave wall or a moving insect. By comparing the timing and direction of each returning echo, it builds a working sense of what surrounds it, moment to moment, without ever needing any light at all.

items.prompt: How does a lava tube, a very different kind of cave, actually form?

options.label: Wave action pounds against a cliff of hardened lava until a hollow opens
options.feedback: That describes how a sea cave forms through mechanical erosion; a lava tube forms in a completely different way, without any wave action at all.

options.label: The outer surface of a lava flow hardens into a crust while the still-molten lava beneath keeps flowing, and once that flow drains away, a hollow tube is left behind
options.feedback: Once the still-molten interior drains onward, the hardened crust is left standing as an empty tube.

options.label: Rising groundwater slowly dissolves a channel through solid lava rock
options.feedback: Dissolving describes how a limestone cave forms; the hardened rock making up a lava tube is not dissolved away by water to create the hollow space.

options.label: Repeated small earthquakes gradually shake a hollow open inside a lava flow
options.feedback: Shaking rock apart bit by bit is not how this hollow space forms; the tube is left empty because the molten interior itself flowed onward and away.

items.ok_line: A hardened crust, left standing over an emptied channel.
items.ko_title: Not waves, not dissolving, not shaking
items.ko_line: Ask what was inside that crust before it hardened, and where that material eventually went.
items.exp_text: As a stream of lava flows across the surface, its outer edges lose heat to the air fastest and harden into a solid crust, while the lava still deep inside stays hot enough to keep flowing onward underneath that crust. Once the source of fresh lava feeding that flow stops or moves elsewhere, the still-molten interior can drain away and continue on its path, leaving the now-empty hardened crust standing as a hollow tube.
